headline: New Hampshire's tight license-plate reader rules draw fresh national attention
dek: As other states revisit automated plate surveillance, New Hampshire's law limits eligible uses and requires most scans to be destroyed within three minutes.
body: New Hampshire's decade-old limits on automated license-plate readers are drawing renewed attention as states around the country debate how much vehicle-tracking technology police should be allowed to use. The New Hampshire Bulletin reported Thursday that Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis recently pointed to the Granite State as a model for tighter rules.

Under RSA 261:75-b, New Hampshire allows automated plate readers for local, county and state law-enforcement agencies, but only for specified purposes such as identifying stolen vehicles, vehicles linked to warrants or serious crimes, and vehicles connected to missing or endangered people. Most plate records must be purged within three minutes unless a scan leads to an arrest, citation, protective-custody action or a missing-person or wanted-person match.

The law also says a reader cannot be capable of recording images of a vehicle's occupants, and a positive match by itself is not enough to justify a traffic stop. Agencies must register the devices with the Department of Safety, train users and follow the statute's limits. Privacy researchers quoted by the Bulletin described the framework as among the nation's most restrictive.

The rules do not eliminate every form of plate-data access. The Bulletin reported that New Hampshire agencies can still use contracts to query databases operated elsewhere, while lawmakers are considering whether additional legislation is needed. The renewed debate comes as states including Florida, Arizona, Connecticut and South Dakota examine limits on systems marketed by companies such as Flock, Axon and Motorola Solutions.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: New Hampshire license-plate reader law draws national attention
seoDescription: New Hampshire's law limits automated license-plate reader use and requires most scans to be destroyed within three minutes.
